♻ ☆ Embedding Capabilities of Neural ODEs
Christian Kuehn, Sara-Viola Kuntz
Neural ordinary differential equations (neural ODEs) are a class of neural networks that have gained particular interest in recent years. We study input-output relations of neural ODEs using dynamical systems theory and prove several results about the exact embedding of maps in different neural ODE architectures in low and high dimensions. The embedding capability of a neural ODE architecture can be increased by adding, for example, affine linear layers or augmenting the phase space. However, there is currently no systematic theory available, and our work contributes towards this goal by developing various embedding results as well as identifying situations where no embedding is possible. Our core mathematical techniques include iterative functional equations, Morse functions, and suspension flows, as well as several further ideas from analysis. Although in practice mostly universal approximation theorems are used, our geometric dynamical systems viewpoint on universal embedding provides a fundamental understanding of why certain neural ODE architectures perform better than others.
♻ ☆ TSGP-2: On the Non-Linearity of Symbolic Regression Problems and How to Exploit It with Model-based Semantic Genetic Programming
Philipp Anthes, Alina Geiger, Martin Briesch, Franz Rothlauf
Model-based variation operators such as the one used in Transformer Semantic Genetic Programming (TSGP) are affected by possible biases of their training data. TSGP is trained on programs generated by Genetic Programming (GP) runs on linear target functions, which leads to a bias toward linear offspring. This bias can hinder search performance on problems that require non-linear solutions. This work has two goals: first, we investigate the linearity of standard benchmark problems including the Feynman and real-world problems. While most of the structure of real-world problems can be well approximated by linear functions, the Feynman problems exhibit varying levels of non-linear structure. Thus, a proper variation operator of a search method should be able to create both types of programs, linear as well as non-linear ones. Second, we propose TSGP-2, which follows the functionality of TSGP but uses as training data programs from GP runs on both linear and non-linear target functions. As a result, the training data includes a lower share of programs that behave linearly. With a higher share of non-linear structures, TSGP-2 outperforms TSGP on problems with non-linear structure, while performing similarly on linear problems. In addition, TSGP-2 is less biased toward linear offspring and is able to propose a higher number of meaningful non-linear offspring earlier during search, which coincides with better solutions. The findings underscore the importance of training data for a learned variation operator and emphasize that the biases of search operators should be aligned with the problems they are applied to.

Human vision and video stereo networks both reuse disparity evidence across time, yet a refresh of the input can invalidate a match formed milliseconds earlier. What tells a system whether an old match still counts? We answer this from limited human data in three steps. First, nine temporal mechanisms share a frozen binocular-energy front end and an equal-capacity readout, so held-out behavior isolates the temporal selection rule: on 240 conditions from 10 observers, down-weighting aged evidence that has lost binocular support lowers subject RMSE from 12.6% to 10.3% and reproduces a period-dependent reversed-depth illusion, across all 59 readings of the unpublished protocol and 8 front-end perturbations. Second, four propositions establish what such data can identify: gating is identified at the level of the refresh schedule, and candidate binding is invisible to standard stimuli but exposed by a single-eye geometry flip that separates the readouts by up to 7.1%. Third, the identified rule becomes a two-field stereo memory that separates sample validity from hypothesis support. It removes a 50 ms recovery lag after geometry flips, and its regime analysis explains why plain integration stays preferable on MPI-Sintel, where 71.1% of pixels change appearance but not disparity.

☆ Online Statistical Inference for Derivative-Free Constrained Stochastic Optimization
Jianliang Ye, Sen Na
We study statistical inference for nonlinear equality-constrained stochastic optimization problems in settings where derivative information is unavailable or expensive to obtain. While recent advances in stochastic sequential quadratic programming (SSQP) have enabled efficient online optimization, existing methods either rely on gradient information or suffer from high computational costs. To address these limitations, we develop a sketched derivative-free SSQP (SDF-SSQP) method that simultaneously achieves computational efficiency and valid statistical inference. By leveraging randomized sketching, the proposed method reduces the per-iteration computational cost to $O((d+m)^2)$, where $d$ is the dimension of the decision variable and $m$ is the number of constraints, making it well suited for large-scale problems. To overcome the challenges that both sketching and zeroth-order approximations introduce for statistical inference, we adopt a random-scaling approach that eliminates the need for explicit estimation of the asymptotic covariance matrix. We establish the asymptotic normality of the averaged primal--dual iterates and construct a self-normalized statistic that is asymptotically pivotal. The resulting inference procedure is fully online, requires neither covariance estimation nor matrix inversion, and incurs an additional per-iteration cost of the same order as that of the optimization update. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in terms of both optimization performance and statistical inference accuracy.

☆ A Kernel Framework for Linear Operator Equations
Damir Filipovic, Valentin Tissot-Daguette
Solving linear operator equations with nonlocal terms or heterogeneous constraints often requires specific numerical schemes. We develop a unified approach based on embedding such equations into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS). Differential, boundary, and integral operators are represented by their Riesz representers in the RKHS. The equations are solved in the regularized least-squares sense at finitely many collocation points. The solution is a finite linear combination of operator-induced representers and is obtained from a single linear system. Its sensitivities, such as financial Greeks, follow by direct differentiation. To reduce the computational cost for large collocation sets, we introduce a Nyström approximation based on subsampling the operator-induced representers. It yields the best approximation of this solution within the reduced trial space, in a regularized empirical norm. Numerical examples cover ordinary, partial, and partial integro-differential equations, including multi-asset and jump-diffusion option pricing.

This paper proposes a framework for sequential Bayesian updating in probabilistic digital twins using data from multiple sources collected over time. The framework distinguishes between property data and behavior data, according to how observations relate to the digital state. Property data directly inform a subset of the uncertain model parameters and can therefore be incorporated using efficient dedicated Bayesian updating methods. Behavior data provide indirect information through the prediction model and require the solution of a Bayesian inverse problem. To reduce the associated computational cost, an active-learning-based surrogate strategy is introduced that evolves with the digital state and adaptively refines the prediction model in regions relevant to posterior inference. The framework is evaluated using an idealized cantilever beam example and a geotechnical case study of a canal wall subject to varying water levels and corrosion. The examples show how complementary data sources, including both equality observations and inequality information from observed system survival, can inform uncertain parameters and system reliability. The proposed surrogate-based updating scheme yields posterior estimates and prediction accuracy comparable to those of physics-based updating while requiring substantially fewer model evaluations. The proposed framework thus supports multi-source updating and reliability assessment in probabilistic digital twins of engineering systems.

First, we consider minimizer localization, where the learner seeks to identify a point within distance $\varepsilon$ of the unique minimizer. We introduce a new instance-dependent quantity $Δ_\varepsilon(f)$, corresponding to the threshold for which the sublevel set of $f-\min f$ has length $2\varepsilon$. We prove a lower bound of order $Δ_\varepsilon(f)^{-2}$ and give a bisection-style algorithm that matches this rate up to logarithmic factors. We then revisit the simple-regret setting, where the goal is to identify an $\varepsilon$-optimal point. Surprisingly, no comparable instance-dependent improvement is possible: every correct algorithm has sample complexity of order $\varepsilon^{-2}$ on every instance, matching the minimax rate up to constants. Together, these results separate the statistical complexity of minimizer localization from that of simple-regret optimization in one-dimensional convex bandits.

On FPGAs, conventional confidence-based exits add arithmetic control paths poorly matched to LUT fabrics, consuming resources that could otherwise support the main datapath. We present ExitLUT, which replaces softmax-style exit decisions with learned Boolean functions mapped directly into FPGA LUTs. ☆ Diagnosing Epistemic Uncertainty in Neural Operators: Effects of Initialization, Discretization, and Function Sampling

Neural operators provide efficient surrogates for mappings between function spaces, but their reliability cannot be characterized by the performance of a single trained model. Existing neural operator uncertainty quantification approaches often characterize predictive uncertainty without separately identifying the contributions of individual sources of epistemic uncertainty. Finite sampling of the training function space, output discretization, and model initialization can produce substantial variation among learned operators even when the underlying physical problem is deterministic. We systematically investigate these sources of epistemic uncertainty across a diverse set of operator learning architectures. Across our experiments, we train approximately 46,000 neural operator models and construct ensembles over training datasets, model initializations, and output discretizations to characterize distributions of relative $L_2$ error rather than individual trained realizations. We find substantial architecture-dependent differences in epistemic uncertainty, with model initialization often accounting for the largest proportion of variance in relative $L_2$ error. The ranked performance of neural operator architectures can invert as the number and spatial distribution of output samples change, with the best architectures under sparse or randomly sampled observations differing from those at higher-resolution or structured discretizations. Furthermore, ensembles that reliably characterize aggregate operator error can provide unreliable estimates of error quantiles for individual test functions. These results highlight the importance of distinguishing the sources of epistemic uncertainty when evaluating neural operator reliability and establishing robust benchmarking practices.

Each sample is mapped to a truncated path signature, capturing the joint geometric structure of its channels, and the coreset is selected by greedily minimizing the Sliced Wasserstein distance between the empirical signature distributions of the candidate subset and the full dataset, a criterion for which we establish a convergence guarantee for random coresets. This advantage generalizes to public UEA regular multivariate time series benchmarks specifically when class-discriminative information is purely geometric.

We establish an ICL framework for path space, using path signature features. Under sparse signature approximation and suitable moment and concentration conditions, we establish finite-sample prediction error bounds. Our analysis goes beyond the IID data setting in the existing ICL theory, allowing dependence among demonstrations and the query. Experiments on in-context sparse recovery, nonlinear path regression, execution-cost prediction, and financial payoff inference demonstrate robustness to changes in observation grids and adaptation to unseen market environments. Across these prediction tasks, transformers with signatures match or outperform vanilla transformer baselines with substantially fewer trainable parameters, highlighting the effectiveness and efficiency of signature-based ICL.

Slay the Spire 2 (STS2) is a single-player deck-building game that requires long-term planning under heavy randomness. We present AlphaDefect, an expert-level AI system for STS2: for each character, one network trained with proximal policy optimization (PPO) makes every decision of a run, in combat and outside it. At the highest difficulty, Ascension 10, on two versions of the game current in November 2026 and on test seeds not played in training, AlphaDefect wins 62-77% of runs across six characters with greedy play and 68-80% with test-time search, after 1.3 to 6.7 billion decisions of training per character; runs uploaded by human players of all levels are won 11-20% of the time at the same difficulty. The networks read the game as entity records that identify each card, relic and enemy through a learned embedding and attributes from the game data, together with consequences of public information computed by the engine. Ablations show how much the agent depends on this encoding: without these identities, the network did not win a single run, and without the computed consequences it won 8.3 points fewer. To our knowledge, AlphaDefect is the strongest publicly reported STS2 agent as of November 2026.

When the PCA keeps every direction of the labeled examples, the examples collapse into a regular simplex in which all pairwise distances are equal. To address this problem, we propose Rotated Frozen Embeddings (RoFE), a training-free method that rotates PCA scores before PFN inference. We theoretically show that rotation makes the column variances nearly equal, so that standardization approximately preserves the embedding geometry. Across image and text classification tasks, encoders, and tabular foundation models, RoFE improves low-data performance over the PCA interface and outperforms baselines that require task-specific training. The improvements also extend to regression.

In this paper, we develop a new method that denoises pairwise distances before using them to construct spectral embeddings and identify communities. Our approach uses cross-fitted projections to estimate distances between the underlying signals, selects a neighborhood radius from the observed sample, and builds a random geometric graph whose spectral coordinates represent the latent geometric structure. By connecting nearby points, such a geometric graph can distinguish different groups even when their centers coincide. A novel recursive procedure is then proposed to extract clusters from the graph using its spectral embeddings when such clusters exist. On the theoretical side, under a manifold model, we provide guarantees for our spectral embedding algorithm, which can be understood through the eigendecomposition of an integral operator associated with the underlying geometry. We show that the algorithm is robust to noise when the total noise energy is comparable to the total signal energy or, under additional conditions, exceeds it. To our knowledge, this is among the first spectral embedding algorithms that can handle such strong noise in datasets with nonlinear structures. In addition, our proposed clustering algorithm can recover the underlying clusters even when their centers coincide. Numerical studies demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed method in mitigating noise and revealing geometric structures for both spectral embedding and clustering.

Under suitable conditions, the upper and lower bounds match up to logarithmic factors. Moreover, wPPRC can achieve a worst-case risk of smaller order than the minimax risks under four baseline observation structures on the same joint distribution class, demonstrating the value of additional pseudo-labels. The VS estimator satisfies an expected-risk oracle inequality and preserves the improvement over the baseline minimax risks with the same total labeled-data budget. Simulations and an application to predicting homeless counts illustrate the gains of the proposed estimators.
☆ Aggregation Rules Induced by KL-Regularised Preference Dynamics on Networks
Milan Vojnovic
We study agents that each align a model to their own preference data while observing one another, and ask which aggregation rule the resulting policies implement. Each round, an agent takes one KL-regularised step. The step involves a reference that the agent is penalised for leaving and a challenger against which its responses are compared, and each of the two may be the agent's own or an average over the agents it observes; attention need not be reciprocal. Aggregating the reference makes the rule collective. Agent $v$ then has the weight $π_v/β_v$, its share of the network's long-run attention divided by its temperature. If, in addition, the challenger is fixed, the agents concentrate on the response maximising $\sum_v(π_v/β_v)r_v(y)$, where $r_v$ is agent $v$'s reward, and the rule is cardinal. If the reference is fixed and the challenger aggregated, the agents' policies at a fixed point generally differ, and any weighted mean of them is an approximate maximal lottery whatever the weights, so the dynamics select no weighting. If both are aggregated, the rule is ordinal: averaged over rounds, the collective policy is a maximal lottery of the influence-weighted preference kernel, up to a slack that we bound. Where a collective rule exists, its weights depend only on the attention weights and the temperatures.

On the contrary, node-level tasks involve dependent nodes, often in a few large graphs. Finally, we apply this framework to several models of GNNs, unifying several existing results on GNNs transferability and universality.

Two consequences follow. Invariance does not identify $PA(Y)$ uniquely, since every descendant-free superset is invariant as well; and $PA(Y)$ is the unique minimal invariant set. In finite samples, recovery requires the non-invariant sets to be separated from invariance by a margin, and the sample size splits into a screening term logarithmic in the ambient dimension and a term inherited from conditional mean embedding estimation, which is the binding one. The characterisation yields two selection rules with different failure modes, of which the conservative one controls false positives. They also show that invariance testing is a practical bottleneck: two natural designs are severely miscalibrated, while the selected test reduces but does not eliminate Type I error inflation.

It is benign if deleting it leaves the effect identifiable in the resulting MPDAG and Markov equivalent explanations agree; the local price is then bounded, and otherwise, for small k, of order sqrt(n). At benign edges the price is of order R+K, with R a ratio of efficient lengths and K a cross-model constant. It equals one, so that honesty is free, exactly when K = 0, generically decided by a d-separation. For two Markov classes it is determined within a factor 3.40, and its upper bound is approached without knowing the base point or the weak edge. A further graphical condition gives the rate uniformly in a second edge's margin.

☆ Operator-Valued Q-Learning: Compositional Bellman Recursions for Order-Sensitive Decision Making
Swagatam Das, Swagato Das
In quantum pulse sequences, spacecraft attitude control and in-hand reorientation, actions act on a hidden physical state as non-commuting operators, so the outcome of a plan depends on the order of its actions. We let the value function carry this structure: each Q(s,a) is an N x N operator, and the Bellman backup applies the action's dual map to the continuation value, Q(s,a) = K_a^*(R(s,a) + gamma E V(s')). Unrolled along a plan, the recursion builds the ordered product of the actions' operators, and the value at any latent state is a linear trace readout. It is exact for policies that do not observe the latent, the backup contracts for unitary and orthogonal dynamics, and an asynchronous operator TD scheme learns it with almost-sure convergence. Classical values live in a lattice, so a maximum over actions exists; self-adjoint operators form an anti-lattice (Kadison) and have none. An operator log-sum-exp still gives one operator per state-action pair whose readout upper-bounds the value of every policy at every latent state. The sampled update converges to it for a finite horizon, and it reduces to soft Q-learning and the QMDP bound when actions commute. We prove that scalar values on observations that ignore action order must confuse swapped histories, that exact history tables grow exponentially for free action groups but polynomially for nilpotent ones, and give a Hankel-rank lower bound on the operator dimension. In experiments the learned policy matches 1000-simulation tree search on SO(3) pointing for horizons up to 20 at ~10^4 times lower decision cost, transfers zero-shot to unseen initial states, and acts exactly on its belief mean when the initial state is hidden, where plugging the mean into a DQN does not. A planner with the same model knowledge is more sample-efficient at short horizons, and a DQN given the operators matches or exceeds OpQ.
☆ Revisiting Continual Learning in Language Models: A Three-Interface Diagnosis of Stability and Plasticity NeurIPS 2026

Continual learning in language models is commonly studied in the incremental learning (IL) setting, where a model learns a sequence of tasks and is evaluated through its final classifier or language-model (LM) head. This interface, however, does not indicate where forgetting occurs: a drop in accuracy may reflect representation degradation in the backbone, readout mismatch in the head, or both. We therefore argue that backward transfer (BWT) and forward transfer (FWT) should be interpreted as interface-dependent quantities rather than as single modellevel properties. We study three evaluation interfaces: the trained head, which is updated sequentially with the backbone; a probe newly trained on frozen backbone features; and a classifier-free backbone diagnostic. They measure deployed performance, recoverability under a new readout, and representation separability, respectively. Across class-incremental experiments with encoder and decoder language backbones, plus task-incremental sanity checks, conclusions about forgetting and plasticity change with the interface: the trained head often indicates severe forgetting, the probe near-complete recoverability, and the backbone diagnostic intermediate representation drift with a consistent negative relation between stability and plasticity. This relation holds for clustering-free diagnostics such as nearest-class-mean accuracy and across five clustering algorithms and three metrics. Finally, Just LM-Head Tuning (JLT), a head-only intervention on a fixed incrementally trained backbone, recovers 96-99% of the gap to joint training for replayand distillation-based methods but only about three quarters for plain sequential fine-tuning, suggesting that many failures attributed to catastrophic forgetting reflect head-backbone mismatch plus partial representation drift. Our results call for reporting where forgetting is measured, not only how much.

Individual heterogeneity and acquisition-site variability complicate neuroimaging-based characterization of autism spectrum disorder (ASD). We propose PsyDrift, combining ASD/healthy-control-supervised functional-connectivity representations with healthy-reference latent diffusion. An encoder produces 128-dimensional representations, and a denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) learns exclusively from healthy training latents. Distance from a diffusion-denoised reconstruction provides a continuous deviation score. We evaluate 1,102 subjects from all 20 ABIDE-I sites using five-seed leave-one-site-out cross-validation. The classifier and DDPM achieve mean-site AUROCs of $0.798 \pm 0.003$ and $0.718 \pm 0.013$, respectively; uncertainties denote seed standard deviations. Matched healthy-reference scorers on the same representation achieve 0.68-0.71; the statistical significance of diffusion's modest numerical advantage remains unestablished. Within ASD, scores show weak associations with ADOS Total (Spearman $ρ= 0.108$, $p = 0.038$) and full-scale IQ ($ρ= -0.138$, $p = 0.002$), without adjustment for age, sex, site, or head motion. Frozen evaluation without retraining or hyperparameter adaptation yields pooled AUROCs of 0.69 on ABIDE-II and 0.61 on ADHD-200, providing preliminary evidence of cross-cohort and cross-disorder transfer. These results demonstrate healthy-reference deviation scoring within an ASD-supervised representation; incremental predictive and clinical value remains unestablished.

☆ The response field approach to path integral control
George Stamatescu
This paper investigates non-linear path integral control problems within the response field formalism of nonequilibrium field theory. The aim of this work is exploratory, based on the identification of correspondences between backward adjoint processes and the response field of non-equilibrium statistical physics, whose properties have not been set out in an optimal control setting. The response field is found to play an analogous role to the backward adjoint process under the stochastic maximum principle. In particular, the gradient of the optimal cost-to-go at the initial time, which is proportional to the optimal control, is given by the average of the response field at the initial time. In contrast to the case of non-equilibrium dynamics, the response function is found to be acausal in the control setting. The linear-quadratic case of path integral control is studied, confirming it as the free theory, meaning that solving the control problem is equivalent to completing the square and determining the propagator for a two point boundary value problem. The developments presented here are a necessary prelude to applications based on field theoretic approximation, for both path integral control and their dual inference problems.

Selecting a strategy by testing it against an opponent is common in game-playing AI, red-teaming of language models, and safety evaluations of AI agents. In many of these settings, the opponent adapts to what it observes, so a strategy that keeps winning in practice may already have stopped working by the time it is used. Motivated by these settings, we study a player who tries strategies in practice games against an adaptive opponent, decides when to stop, and then either selects one strategy for the next game or abstains. The goal is to select a strategy that meets a target win probability while rarely selecting one that has already fallen below it. For a single strategy, we propose the Sequential Private Accumulated-excess Rule (SPAR), which accumulates evidence through a capped likelihood ratio and selects the strategy once this evidence reaches a privately drawn uniform threshold. We show that the stopping time must involve such private randomness. The number of games SPAR needs is inversely proportional to the error tolerance, and this rate is optimal even when the opponent happens not to adapt. To select among multiple strategies, we introduce Screen-then-SPAR, which screens candidates in stages before applying SPAR. The procedure adapts to the best strategy's unknown initial margin above the target and achieves the minimax rate up to logarithmic factors. The performance of Screen-then-SPAR is demonstrated through simulations and two real-data studies, one using recorded coding-agent attacks from MonitoringBench and the other using rock-paper-scissors matches between human players and an adaptive bot.

☆ Statistically Optimal and Near Linear Time Hypothesis Selection
Satyen Kale, Amirreza Shaeiri, Kunal Talwar
In hypothesis selection we are given $n$ distributions $q_1,\dots,q_n$ on a countable domain $\mathcal{X}$ and samples from an unknown distribution $p$. The goal is a distribution $q$ with $\mathrm{TV}(p,q)\leα\min_i\mathrm{TV}(p,q_i)+ε$. The factor $α=2$ is optimal for algorithms using a number of samples from $p$ that is independent of $|\mathcal{X}|$, and in general only improper learners achieve it. We give a learner that achieves $α=2$ with $O(\log(n/δ)/ε^2)$ samples of $p$, with probability at least $1-δ$. This matches the sample complexity of Yatracos's factor-$3$ estimator, and it removes the logarithmic factors in the factor-$2$ bound of Bousquet et al. (FOCS 2021). The learner accesses the $q_i$ only through sampling and pointwise comparisons. We measure its running time by its oracle complexity, the number of oracle calls. In expectation it makes $O((nε^{-2}+ε^{-4}\log(1/ε))\log(n/δ))$ oracle calls, independent of $\mathcal{X}$. It runs multiplicative weights over the constraints $\mathrm{TV}(q,q_i)\le\mathrm{TV}(p,q_i)$ and uses at most one sample of $p$ per round.
♻ ☆ Perfect Clustering in Extremely Sparse Multilayer Networks with Groupwise Subspace Structure
Marianna Pensky
The paper studies a multilayer network on the same collection of nodes, where each layer follows the Generalized Random Dot Product Graph Model. Furthermore, all layers can be partitioned into groups, each group with its own unique latent subspace structure, but otherwise the matrices of connection probabilities can all be different. This setting is extremely general and includes most multilayer network models as special cases. In addition, we are interested in the situation where the layer networks may be extremely sparse and, therefore, the layer-by-layer analysis is unreliable. This problem can also be seen as a generalization of the classic setting in which one recovers a shared structure across an entire collection of matrices, extending it to the case where such structures are shared only within specific groups of matrices. The key task in this setting is to recover the groups of layers with unique subspace structures, since, after that, the information in those groups of layers can be pooled together by well-studied methods. Until now, clustering of layers in such networks was based on layer-by-layer analysis, which required the multilayer network to be sufficiently dense. Our paper is the first to provide a tensor-based approach to the problem that combines information from all layers in an unconventional manner. Our theoretical results, established under intuitive and non-restrictive assumptions, assert that the new technique achieves perfect clustering under sparsity conditions that, up to logarithmic factors, coincide with the computational lower bound derived for a much simpler model. The paper also delivers a nuanced message about the applicability of the new technique.

♻ ☆ Flexible Matrix Estimation with Side Information
Anish Agarwal, Jungjun Choi, Ming Yuan
We introduce a flexible framework for high-dimensional matrix estimation to incorporate side information for both rows and columns. Existing approaches, such as inductive matrix completion, often impose restrictive structure---for example, an exact low-rank covariate interaction term, linear covariate effects, and limited ability to exploit components explained only by one side (row or column) or by neither---and frequently omit an explicit noise component. To address these limitations, we propose to decompose the underlying matrix as the sum of four complementary components: (possibly nonlinear) interaction between row and column characteristics; row characteristic-driven component, column characteristic-driven component, and residual low-rank structure unexplained by observed characteristics. By combining sieve-based projection with nuclear-norm penalization, each component can be estimated separately and these estimated components can then be aggregated to yield a final estimate. We derive Frobenius- and entrywise-norm convergence rates that demonstrate the robustness of our estimator across a broad range of model configurations with varying degrees of informativeness in the side information. We further extend the method to partially observed matrices under both missing-at-random and missing-not-at-random mechanisms, including block-missing patterns motivated by causal panel data. Simulations and a real-data application to tobacco sales show that leveraging side information improves imputation accuracy and can enhance treatment-effect estimation relative to standard low-rank and spectral-based alternatives.

We introduce "causal pieces", a novel concept for analysing spiking neural networks (SNNs), inspired by "linear pieces" used to study expressivity and trainability in artificial neural networks (ANNs). Causal pieces partition the input and parameter space of a feedforward SNN with single-spike coding into distinct regions where the same subnetwork causes the output spikes. For networks of current-based leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neurons with large membrane time constants, we show that within each causal piece, output spike times are locally Lipschitz continuous with respect to inputs and network parameters. We further prove a lower bound on the approximation error that depends on the number of causal pieces. Thus, the number of causal pieces is a measure of the approximation capabilities of SNNs, which is valid despite spike-time discontinuities and applies to networks with both excitatory and inhibitory synapses. Empirically, we find that parameter initialisations yielding more causal pieces on the training set strongly correlate with SNN training success across multiple benchmarks, including Yin-Yang, Fashion-MNIST, and EuroSAT. Moreover, simulations with standard single-spike LIF neurons indicate that our findings extend beyond the theoretically analysed regime. These results establish causal pieces as a powerful and principled tool for analysing and improving the computational capabilities of SNNs.

Francesca R. Crucinio, Sahani Pathiraja
We consider the problem of sampling from a probability distribution $π$. It is well known that this can be written as an optimisation problem over the space of probability distribution in which we aim to minimise the Kullback--Leibler divergence from $π$. We consider several partial differential equations (PDEs) whose solution is a minimiser of the Kullback--Leibler divergence from $π$ and connect them to well-known Monte Carlo algorithms. We focus in particular on PDEs obtained by considering the Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao geometry over the space of probabilities and show that these lead to a natural implementation using importance sampling and sequential Monte Carlo. ♻ ☆ Generalized Guarantees for Variational Inference in the Presence of Even and Elliptical Symmetry
Charles C. Margossian, Isaac E. Rankin, Lawrence K. Saul
Variational inference (VI) approximates a target density $p$ by the best match $q$ in a family $\mathcal Q$ of tractable distributions. The variational approximation is found by minimizing a divergence, most commonly the reverse Kullback-Leibler divergence $\text{KL}(q||p)$, although other divergences can be considered. In practice, $p \notin \mathcal Q$ and so the optimal variational approximation is misspecified. Despite this misspecification, it was recently shown that the minimizer of $\text{KL}(q||p)$ is guaranteed to recover the mean in the presence of even symmetry and likewise the correlation matrix in the presence of elliptical symmetry for a log-concave target $p$. We extend this result in several directions. First, we relax the assumption of log-concavity and instead merely require $p$ to be unimodal, allowing for heavy-tailed targets. Second, we obtain guarantees for cases where $p$ exhibits symmetry along some but not all of its coordinates. These partial symmetries arise naturally in Bayesian hierarchical models, where the prior induces a challenging geometry but still possesses axes of symmetry. Third, we extend these guarantees to $f$-divergences, a broad class which includes the forward and reverse-KL divergences and the $α$-divergences.
♻ ☆ Efficient Cost-Aware LLM Evaluation via Bayesian Bandit Gittins Indices ICML 2026
Qian Xie, Yueli He, Nairen Cao
Exhaustively evaluating every candidate LLM configuration on every benchmark item to identify a high-performing one is costly. We formulate configuration selection as a cost-aware Bayesian bandit problem and propose GittinsEval, inspired by Bayesian-optimal Gittins-index policies for Markov chain selection. We augment this policy with a separate anytime recommendation rule over both fully and partially evaluated configurations, using an LCB-style score to account for posterior uncertainty. GittinsEval is computationally efficient, requiring only lightweight online updates after offline precomputation. Across tasks with varying numbers of candidates and examples, GittinsEval is consistently competitive, with particularly strong gains over the Bayesian optimization baselines on few-candidate large-example benchmarks and over cost-unaware frequentist baselines on large-candidate tasks. Crucially, GittinsEval often attains near-zero simple regret using only 1%-2% of the exhaustive-evaluation cost; it also offers a stopping rule that typically triggers at 1%-10% with an appropriate cost--quality tradeoff parameter.

Across the eight benchmarks, CC-Gittins recovers a substantial fraction of the true Pareto frontier at roughly 10% of the exhaustive-evaluation cost, and recovers most of the frontier with few false positives by 30%.

Despite strong empirical performance, theoretical understanding of this approach remains limited: existing guarantees are often asymptotic or entail prohibitive computational costs in the worst case. In this paper, we address this gap by studying sparse recovery from a small number of linear measurements, a classical problem in compressed sensing. We show that, given an accurate diffusion model capturing a sparsity-promoting Bernoulli-Gaussian prior, a likelihood-guided annealed Langevin sampler provably recovers the sparse signal in polynomial time with near-optimal sample complexity for a broad family of random and deterministic sensing matrices. When the signal is indeed drawn from the postulated prior, we further establish total variation guarantees for posterior sampling after a final denoising step. These results lay a theoretical foundation for statistically and computationally efficient inverse solvers with diffusion priors.

On these data, seven choices each changed a reported result with model families fixed. Row-level splits inflate our best score by 0.31 macro-averaged F1 over held-out files, where matched-dimensionality classical and quantum models barely clear chance. Under its own white-box attack the quantum kernel's score falls from 0.56 to 0.01 (chance 0.50), while a transferred attack in the same run leaves 0.52. Trees admit no gradient-based white-box attack, so their attacked scores are upper bounds. These attack results use eight-dimension detectors under row-level splits. On gas-pipeline and simulated-grid data, neither quantum detector is more accurate or consistently more robust; three of the seven choices reproduce fully on gas data with one pressure feature log-scaled (two within noise), and none of the four checked on the grids does. Benchmarks should hold out whole files and give every model its own attack where possible. We release code and checklist.

In this paper, we theoretically analyze practical algorithms of dataset distillation applied to the gradient-based training of two-layer neural networks with width $L$. By focusing on a non-linear task structure called multi-index model, we prove that the low-dimensional structure of the problem is efficiently encoded into the resulting distilled data. This dataset reproduces a model with high generalization ability for a required memory complexity of $\tildeΘ$$(r^2d+L)$, where $d$ and $r$ are the input and intrinsic dimensions of the task. To the best of our knowledge, this is one of the first theoretical works that include a specific task structure, leverage its intrinsic dimensionality to quantify the compression rate and study dataset distillation implemented solely via gradient-based algorithms.

Fairness interventions often targets disparities associated with a single sensitive attribute in binary classification tasks. We refer to these unintended effects as cross-attribute externalities of fairness. We study how fairness with respect to one sensitive attribute varies when an initially unfair classification or regression model is corrected with respect to another attribute. This highlights a limitation of conventional fairness evaluation, in which the success of an intervention is assessed mainly for the attribute it targets. In a jointly Gaussian model, we derive explicit trajectories for marginal and joint disparities and identify conditions under which an intervention eliminates disparities with respect to its target attribute while increasing disparities associated with another attribute. We also derive sharp partial-identification bounds on the resulting externalities when a sensitive attribute is unavailable and extend our results to categorical sensitive attributes. We illustrate these externalities using classification and regression real-data: in the classification experiments, interventions increase unfairness with respect to the hidden attribute in the majority of scenarios across more than half of the datasets considered; in the regression experiments on the ACSIncome dataset, correcting for race reduces sex disparities, whereas subsequently correcting for age increases them.

We show that the off-span norm implicitly selected by affine EI can lead to underexploration, and SABLE instead prescribes it using an exploration schedule, without restricting search to a learned subspace. An efficient recompression scheme reduces information to $\mathcal O(M)$ pseudo-observations, bringing the overall time complexity per step to $\mathcal O(M^2D+M^3+D\log D)$ while keeping parameter inference, prediction, and acquisition decisions to tens of milliseconds. By capturing the complex biochemical interactions within a cell, these networks provide a functional map of disease progression that goes beyond simple genomic mutations. Consequently, the development of specific signaling models of patients has significant relevance, allowing for a more granular representation of individual disease profiles. In this setting, there is a growing need for robust methodologies capable of comparing graph based pathway structures to identify similarities and differences across patient cohorts. Such comparisons are essential for the identification of clinically meaningful subgroups, and the discovery of novel biomarkers. Standard graph kernels, while mathematically rigorous, often remain too generic for this purpose. They frequently fail to capture features specific to gene signaling networks, resulting in suboptimal clustering performance. In this paper, we present a domain specific graph kernel designed for mechanistic signaling networks. Unlike generic approaches, our method explicitly incorporates biological constraints and gene interaction patterns into the kernel formulation, enabling a more accurate characterization of both topological structure and functional behavior. We assess its performance on breast cancer datasets, focusing on its ability to support disease subtyping. Our results suggest that our approach can effectively contribute to patient stratification.
♻ ☆ The Loss Does Not See the Basis, but Adam Does
Devender Singh
Different optimization algorithms can find very different solutions to the same problem. Gradient descent (GD) exhibits a low-rank bias in overparameterized problems when initialized near zero, while Adam does not. GD is rotationally equivariant: rotating both factors of a factored model $W = UV^\top$ by an orthogonal matrix leaves the loss unchanged, and GD's solution rotates accordingly. In contrast, Adam is not. We show that any algorithm using only the current gradient and respecting rotational symmetry amounts to a left-preconditioner depending only on the gradient's Gram matrix. This gives a norm-based test, which passes for the spectral norm in Muon and fails for Adam's $\ell_\infty$ norm. Empirically, nine optimizers fall into groups consistent with the test on underdetermined matrix sensing. Sharing Adam's second moment across coordinates gradually recovers a low-rank bias, and its solutions approach GD's as the stepsize decreases. On four hyperspectral scenes, Adam's solutions are hundreds to thousands of times further from GD's than two GD runs with different step sizes are from each other. In transformers and LoRA adapters, Adam separates two rotationally equivalent models from the first iteration, and learns higher-rank attention updates. Overall, recovering particular solutions depends on the optimizer's invisible coordinate basis, as well as how fast it grows small singular values relative to large ones.
comment: v2: revised and expanded. Code: https://github.com/idevender/loss-basis-adam
♻ ☆ Optimal Rate of Kernel Regression in Large Dimensions
Weihao Lu, Haobo Zhang, Yicheng Li, Manyun Xu, Qian Lin
We perform a study on kernel regression for large-dimensional data (where the sample size $n$ is polynomially depending on the dimension $d$ of the samples, i.e., $n\asymp d^γ$ for some $γ>0$ ). We first build a general tool to characterize the upper bound and the minimax lower bound of kernel regression for large dimensional data through the Mendelson complexity $\varepsilon_{n}^{2}$ and the metric entropy $\bar{\varepsilon}_{n}^{2}$ respectively. When the target function falls into the RKHS associated with a (general) inner product model defined on $\mathbb{S}^{d}$, we utilize the new tool to show that the minimax rate of the excess risk of kernel regression is $n^{-1/2}$ when $n\asymp d^γ$ for $γ=2, 4, 6, 8, \cdots$. We then further determine the optimal rate of the excess risk of kernel regression for all the $γ>0$ and find that the curve of optimal rate varying along $γ$ exhibits several new phenomena including the multiple descent behavior and the periodic plateau behavior. As an application, For the neural tangent kernel (NTK), we also provide a similar explicit description of the curve of optimal rate. As a direct corollary, we know these claims hold for wide neural networks as well.
♻ ☆ Rare Event Analysis via Stochastic Optimal Control
Yuanqi Du, Jiajun He, Dinghuai Zhang, Eric Vanden-Eijnden, Carles Domingo-Enrich
Rare events, from biomolecular conformational changes and phase transitions to chemical reactions, are central to many physical systems, yet extremely difficult to study computationally because unbiased simulations seldom produce them. Transition Path Theory provides a rigorous statistical framework for analyzing such events: it characterizes the ensemble of reactive trajectories between two metastable states (reactant and product), and its central object, the committor function (the probability that the system next reaches the product rather than the reactant), encodes essential kinetic and thermodynamic information. We introduce a framework for committor estimation that builds on stochastic optimal control, with a principled formulation that grounds committor learning on capped hitting-time trajectories. In this framework the committor defines a feedback control, proportional to the gradient of its logarithm, that steers trajectories toward the reactive region, enabling sampling of reactive paths. As practical algorithms, we develop two training losses: a heuristic on-policy direct backpropagation loss and a principled off-policy Value Matching loss, for which we establish first-order optimality guarantees. Being off-policy, Value Matching can leverage simulated trajectories from alternative sampling processes and reuse them from a replay buffer, which enables efficient learning. In particular, we derive a reactive current-preserving sampling process that can accelerate exploration. On reversible and non-reversible dynamics, the framework yields more accurate committor estimates, reaction rates, and transition path samples than existing methods.
♻ ☆ Online Inference for Quantile Distributional Reinforcement Learning
Zijie Cheng, Zhihua Zhang
In this work, we initiate a systematic study of online statistical inference for quantile-based distributional policy evaluation, which aims to characterize the distribution of discounted cumulative rewards under a given policy. To obtain a finite-dimensional representation of the return distribution, we consider the fixed point $\bmη_m$ of the quantile-projected distributional Bellman equation, parameterized by the quantile vector $\bmθ_m$. We develop two online inference procedures for $\bmθ_m$, covering synchronous and asynchronous sampling from a generative model as well as Markovian data. The first method uses the trajectory of quantile temporal-difference learning (QTD). We establish functional central limit theorems for the partial sums of QTD iterates and construct a recursively computable random-scaling statistic. The resulting confidence intervals have asymptotically exact coverage at deterministic times, with length of order $T^{-1/2}$ in probability. The second method constructs anytime-valid confidence intervals directly from samples. We invert multiscale tests of the Bellman estimating equation and use dyadic reward histograms to evaluate conservative evidence bounds online. The resulting intervals have finite-sample simultaneous coverage, and the histogram contribution to their length bound is of order $T^{-ζ}$ for $ζ\in[1/2,1)$. Under positive limiting state-visit frequencies, the resulting confidence intervals have lengths of order $\sqrt{\log\log T/T}$, which we establish as classwise optimal through a matching lower bound. Together, these results provide complementary guarantees for online inference in quantile distributional reinforcement learning, combining asymptotically exact fixed-time inference with finite-sample anytime validity.
♻ ☆ RL unknotter, hard unknots and unknotting number
Anne Dranowski, Yura Kabkov, Daniel Tubbenhauer
We train a reinforcement learning agent to simplify hard unknot diagrams and pair it with a learned crossing selector to search for short unknotting sequences. Four examples found by the agent lead to two infinite families of prime two-bridge and Montesinos knots of unknotting number three whose connected sums with the figure-eight knot also have unknotting number three, and fifteen new unknotting upper bounds were found on the set of prime knots up to 13 crossings.

♻ ☆ A Trust-Region Interior-Point Stochastic Sequential Quadratic Programming Method
Yuchen Fang, Jihun Kim, Sen Na, James Demmel, Javad Lavaei
In this paper, we propose a trust-region interior-point stochastic sequential quadratic programming (TR-IP-SSQP) method for solving optimization problems with a stochastic objective and deterministic nonlinear equality and inequality constraints. In this setting, exact evaluations of the objective function and its gradient are unavailable, but their stochastic estimates can be constructed. In particular, at each iteration our method builds stochastic oracles whose estimates of the objective value and gradient satisfy proper adaptive accuracy conditions with a fixed probability. To handle inequality constraints, we adopt an interior-point method (IPM), in which the barrier parameter is taken from a prescribed decreasing sequence and is reduced once a stochastic stationarity test is passed. Under standard assumptions, we show that, almost surely, the KKT residual vanishes along the iterations at which the barrier parameter is reduced, and every limit point of these iterates is a KKT point. We implement the method on a subset of problems from the CUTEst test set, as well as on constrained logistic regression problems, to demonstrate its practical performance.

Computer Science and Game Theory
☆ Less Rational, More Transparent: Censorship as (Robustly) Optimal Disclosure
Yiding Feng, Chien-Ju Ho, Wei Tang, Tianze Wei
Online platforms often control the information behind user decisions they want to influence, such as whether a driver accepts a trip or a buyer completes a purchase. A classical result in information disclosure shows that a {\em censorship} policy is optimal for the platform: the platform pools all sufficiently favorable options under a common message, such as a quality badge, and reveals the rest individually. This result, however, presumes fully rational users. We study disclosure to boundedly rational users who follow the logit quantal response model and whose rationality level the platform may not know. Our results deliver a unifying message: less rational, more transparent. Neither bounded rationality nor uncertainty about it calls for a more complex policy; each changes only how much the platform should pool, and only toward greater transparency. When the rationality level is known, censorship remains optimal, and less rational users optimally receive at least as much information as more rational ones. When the rationality level is unknown, censorship remains robustly optimal under each of three criteria: the maximin ratio, maximin payoff, and minimax regret, and the robust censorship can be chosen to be at least as transparent as the policy designed for fully rational users. This additional transparency weakly benefits both parties and acts as insurance against behavioral uncertainty: rationality-robust censorship secures at least 89.96\% of the payoff attainable with knowledge of the user's rationality level, whereas the policy designed for fully rational users can secure as little as 50\%. Taken together, these results suggest that platforms can keep their badge-based disclosure but should narrow its coverage when users may be boundedly rational.

♻ ☆ Attractors Is All You Need: Parity Games In Polynomial Time
Rick van der Heijden
This paper provides a polynomial-time algorithm for solving parity games that runs in $\mathcal{O}(n^{2}\cdot(n + m))$ time-ending a search that has taken decades. Unlike previous attractor-based algorithms, the presented algorithm only removes regions with a determined winner. The paper introduces a new type of attractor that can guarantee finding the minimal dominion of a parity game. The attractor runs in polynomial time and can peel the graph empty.
comment: I withdraw this preprint because the algorithm is incorrect. Tom van Dijk provided a four-vertex counterexample, Odd owns all four vertices, labelled by priority. The moves $0\to1\to2\to4$ are forced; from 4, Odd chooses 0 or 2. Even wins every play, yet for d=4 the first pruning step discards the entire Even dominion, contradicting Lemma 3. The claimed polynomial-time result does not follow
♻ ☆ Participation Incentives in Online Cooperative Games AAMAS 2026
Haris Aziz, Yuhang Guo, Zhaohong Sun
We study cooperative games in which the coalition forms online and the value it generates must be distributed irrevocably among the players present at each time step. We study participation incentives through four axioms: no player gains by delaying their arrival, every newly arriving player who adds value is rewarded immediately, every earlier player whose presence is essential receives a strictly positive share of the new increment, and a player who is a dummy in the current coalition has received nothing. We show that an equal-sharing rule can satisfy all four axioms but requires exponentially many value queries. This barrier is unavoidable as we prove that no equal-sharing rule satisfying the four axioms can be computed exactly with polynomially many value queries. In contrast, weighted sharing rules resolve the issue. For a family of rules that share each increment among a sharing set selected by a greedy deletion scan in reverse arrival order, we characterize exactly the weights under which the four axioms hold. Every rule in this family needs only $O(n^2)$ value queries, and among the desired rules, a unique one has weights that Lorenz-dominate those of all others. We finally characterize a more general class of weighted sharing rules, termed ordinal weighted sharing rules, whose weights depend only on the arrival order and on comparisons between coalition values, that satisfy the four axioms.
comment: Extended version of the AAMAS 2026 conference paper, with new results on weighted sharing rules, query complexity, and characterizations. Compared with v1, this version corrects a notation typo in the definition of S-STAY, an imprecise statement of the theorem on the IR refinement, and a minor error in the definition of IR-eULMES
♻ ☆ Combatting Fraud in Artificial Currency Based Government Benefits Programs
Devansh Jalota, Matthew Tsao, Marco Pavone
Benefits programs are policy tools for providing targeted aid, such as food assistance or transit subsidies. However, these programs are often susceptible to misreporting fraud, wherein users misreport private attributes to obtain excess aid. To address this problem, we introduce a two-stage audit game between an administrator and users in which the administrator can audit users at a cost and levy fines on misreporting users, with player payoff structures designed to reflect real-world benefits programs. We show that the administrator's least-favorable Bayesian Stackelberg equilibria can be computed tractably via linear programming and derive prescriptive bounds on the administrator's excess payments and users' misreporting probability as functions of audit costs and fines. We further establish that, with an appropriately chosen budget level, the reduction in excess payments in any least-favorable Bayesian Stackelberg equilibrium offsets the audit budget required to sustain the mechanism, yielding total costs no greater than those of a baseline without an auditing authority, which we corroborate through a case study of Washington D.C.'s federal transit benefits program.

☆ Set-based comprehensive learning and particle swarm optimization with memory for discrete optimization problem
Yuta Chikuba, Takahiro Hino, Michiharu Maeda
This paper describes a novel algorithm of set-based comprehensive learning and particle swarm optimization with memory for discrete optimization problem. Our algorithm is an approach of searching for the best position in a set by referring to the current position when updating the solution. In order to show the validity of our algorithm, we examine numerical experiments compared to existing algorithms.

☆ Differential evolution with perturbation for continuous function optimization
Takuya Muto, Michiharu Maeda
This paper presents differential evolution with perturbation (DEP) for continuous function optimization. Differential evolution is a simple and efficient algorithm. Perturbation is the phenomenon that the motion by the contribution of the main force is disturbed by the influence subsidiary power. ☆ Sharp Asymptotic Theory of Maximum Likelihood Estimation for Gaussian Processes with a Matern Kernel
Ameer Qaqish, Sudipto Banerjee, Didong Li
Gaussian processes (GPs) provide a flexible framework for modeling complex dependence structures through a covariance function, or kernel, whose parameters determine the variability, correlation, and smoothness of the underlying process. The Matérn kernel is among the most popular choices due to its flexibility in modeling different degrees of smoothness. Although the identifiability of Matérn kernel parameters under fixed-domain asymptotics is completely understood, identifiability alone does not establish the consistency or asymptotic behavior of the maximum likelihood estimators (MLEs) routinely used in practice. In this paper, we address this gap by developing a sharp asymptotic theory for the joint MLE of Matérn kernel parameters. Since parameter identifiability depends critically on the dimension of the observation domain, we characterize the estimable parameters and establish their convergence rates across different dimensions. We establish joint asymptotic normality and minimax optimality of the convergence rates. In addition, we establish asymptotically valid confidence regions for the estimable parameters. Our results accommodate irregular sampling designs and extend to sub-Gaussian measurement errors. Extensive simulation studies illustrate the theoretical results.
☆ Tabular Foundation Models for Weighted Regression and Classification
Junwen Xia, Yan He, Dehan Kong, Zhenhua Lin
Weighted regression and classification have applications ranging from missing-data analysis and causal inference to insurance pricing and particle physics. Existing weighted methods must be fitted and tuned on each dataset, which is costly for flexible nonlinear learners. Tabular foundation models avoid this cost. A Transformer is pretrained once on many simulated datasets and then predicts on a new dataset by in-context learning, using its observations as context without further fitting. Recent models such as TabPFN-3.5 surpass tuned conventional methods, but they cannot use sample weights. We develop a general pipeline that adapts such models to weighted prediction through weighted attention, a normalized weighted loss, and pretraining on synthetic weighted prediction tasks from missing-data problems. Applied to TabPFN-3.5, it yields WeightedPFN, which performs strongly on real datasets, both in missing-data problems and in out-of-distribution causal tasks, while running about as fast as linear baselines. We also establish a statistical theory showing that a suitably pretrained weighted Transformer attains the nonparametric minimax rate for weighted regression on new datasets without further fitting.
☆ Constrained Diffusion from Binary Evaluations via Learned Doob h-Functions
Ssaumya Kammal Jaiswal, Mahfuza Farooque
Conditional generation under constraints that can only be checked on a finished sample, such as a molecular property filter, remains challenging for diffusion models: most guidance methods require differentiable measurement operators, paired conditional data, or rollouts of the base model at every step. We present a framework grounded in the Doob $h$-transform that reduces conditional generation to learning a single function, the probability that a noisy sample denoises into the constraint set. We learn this function from binary clean-sample evaluations alone, by squared-error regression on forward-noised labels; the base model is frozen, one lightweight head is trained per constraint, and noisy-state classifier guidance arises as a special case. The exact guidance step fades where the constraint signal provably vanishes and carries a factor of the inverse probability across samples, which normalized guidance discards: with the schedule and mean step size held fixed, equalizing the step costs 17.0 to 18.5 points of constraint satisfaction on CIFAR-10 at comparable FID, across independently trained estimators. Guidance is more than 50$\times$ cheaper per satisfying sample than rejection sampling at a 1.7% base rate, raises a Lipinski-type property filter on QM9 from 54.3% to 96.8%, and lifts satisfaction on Stable Diffusion 1.5 from 7.2% to 60.0% at one sixteenth of the cost of derivative-free selection, which reaches 9.0%. These results demonstrate that binary evaluations of clean samples are sufficient supervision for constrained generation across pixel, latent, and molecular diffusion.

☆ Selecting Stable Sampling Dynamics for Compositional Diffusion: A Feynman-Kac Weight Reduction
Sunjin Kim, Sungsoo Ahn, Michael Chertkov
Given $K$ separately trained diffusion models, how should one sample from a $β_k$-weighted product of their terminal laws without jointly retraining the experts? Existing Feynman--Kac constructions provide many weighted stochastic differential equations (SDEs) with the correct target marginal. The consequential question is how to select useful proposal dynamics among them. We study an explicit family of weighted diffusions that realizes the same product-of-intermediate-experts trajectory. A scalar parameter $λ$ controls how strongly the proposal drift follows the composed expert score, while an additional Langevin component can be varied independently. Writing $B=\sum_{k=1}^{K}β_k>0$, we identify the distinguished choice $λ=1/B$. At this value, the aggregate squared-score term in the instantaneous Feynman--Kac log-weight rate cancels exactly. For positive expert exponents, the remaining score-disagreement contribution is non-positive. We call this structural cancellation Feynman--Kac reduction. Under bounded-divergence assumptions, it yields an upper bound on the instantaneous unnormalized log-weight rate for all $λ\leq 1/B$. For linear diffusion protocols with compactly supported expert data, $λ=1/B$ yields two-sided bounds at every nonterminal time, for exponents of either sign. A corresponding result holds for a single expert under the same divergence assumption. In these two-sided settings, the selected value is unique within the specified family in a universal worst-case sense. Experiments on Gaussian mixtures and molecular sampling compare the analytically predicted stability with actual sampling quality, including instances in which parameter choices different from $λ=1/B$ perform better empirically.
☆ probly: Uncertainty-Aware Machine Learning
Paul Hofman, Clemens Damke, Timo Löhr, Santo M. A. R. Thies, Alireza Javanmardi, Valentin Margraf, Jakub Paplham, Yusuf Sale, Eyke Hüllermeier, Maximilian Muschalik
As machine learning systems are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, the question of how to represent and quantify uncertainty has moved from a methodological side issue to a central concern. In practice, however, making a model uncertainty-aware is still surprisingly difficult: relevant tools tend to be scattered across libraries, each tied to a particular framework and a particular approach to modeling uncertainty, and the choice of representation, quantification, and evaluation is typically left to the user without much guidance. In this paper, we present probly, a Python package that addresses these issues in a single, modular framework. probly offers (i) lightweight transformations that turn existing models into uncertainty-aware ones, currently supporting PyTorch, scikit-learn, and Flax, (ii) several representations, including second-order distributions, credal sets, and conformal prediction, (iii) the corresponding quantification measures, and (iv) a number of evaluation protocols, which can be combined more or less arbitrarily. Using probly, we conduct a benchmark study on three standard tasks --- selective prediction, out-of-distribution detection, and active learning. In addition, and unlike existing benchmarks, we evaluate suitable methods on first-order data, i.e., datasets for which the target itself is a distribution over outcomes. We further illustrate the flexibility of the package on a number of less standard case studies, including large language models, graph neural networks, and data streams. The package is publicly available at https://github.com/pwhofman/probly.
☆ Grammar Sparsity Sets How Transformers Learn Random Languages NeurIPS 2026
Edgar Andres Hernandez Moreno, Francesco Cagnetta
We study language acquisition by transformers trained on the Random Language Model: a synthetic hierarchical grammar with random production rules, whose sparsity is controlled by a single parameter and whose conditional entropies are known exactly. On depth-two grammars, we find that sparsity sets both the order and the speed of learning. Dense grammars are learnt one level at a time: a token is predicted from its sibling after $t\propto V$ steps and from the full context only after $t\propto V^{3}$, so the two stages are separated by a plateau that widens with $V$. Sparse grammars are learnt all at once, at $t\propto\sqrt V$, with a smaller exponent than even the first stage of a dense one. The exponents $1$ and $1/2$ already appear at depth one, where we derive them for a linear model trained with Adam.

☆ How Multi-Timescale Memory Cools Optimization: Theory and Evidence from AdEMAMix
Jacopo Graldi, Antonio Orvieto, Anastasia Koloskova
Augmenting AdamW with multiple momentum timescales improves large language model pretraining, yet the mechanism driving these gains remains poorly understood. We identify an interaction between multi-timescale optimizer memory and the geometry of normalized networks: memory changes parameter norms and thereby controls how fast parameters rotate. Starting from exact norm dynamics under decoupled weight decay, we show that the parameter norm depends on the temporal correlation of the updates, with weight decay controlling how long these correlations influence optimization. We show how an independently weighted slow momentum can substantially increase the norm of parameters, while contributing negligible power to the instantaneous update, therefore acting as an endogenous annealing schedule. We study this mechanism in AdEMAMix for language-model pretraining. Controlled interventions show that this scheduling mechanism has clear practical consequences and is an important factor behind AdEMAMix's advantage over AdamW.
♻ ☆ Improved Generalization Bounds for Transductive Learning by Transductive Local Complexity and Its Applications ICML 2025
Yingzhen Yang
We study the extension of Transductive Local Complexity (TLC)~\citep{yang2025a-concentration-sampling-without-replacement} as a general tool for analyzing the generalization performance of transductive learning methods. Building on earlier localized complexity methods for transductive learning, the TLC framework was introduced in our prior work. We extend its concentration analysis to general training and test sample sizes through chain analysis and entropy inequalities underlying the exponential Efron Stein inequality. These inequalities are applied to the supremum of the difference between test and training losses and its companion process over the squared function class, then averaged over independent uniform relabeling. Combining these concentration bounds with the peeling strategy, expectation decomposition, and surrogate variance operator yields excess risk bounds nearly consistent with classical Local Rademacher Complexity (LRC) bounds up to a logarithmic gap. We further advance the analysis of transductive learning through two applications: (1) for realizable transductive learning over binary-valued function classes with finite VC dimension $\dVC$ and $u \ge m \ge \dVC$, where $u$ and $m$ are the numbers of test features and training features, Theorem 6.1 gives a TLC bound for a single static empirical risk minimizer of order $O(d^{\textup{(VC)}} \log(me/\dVC)/m)$ at any fixed confidence level, improving the logarithmic complexity term in the known ERM bound under a uniform random split from $\log n$ to $\log m$, and (2) Theorem 6.2 presents a sharper excess risk bound for transductive kernel learning compared to the prior local complexity-based result.

♻ ☆ A Unified Comparative Study with Generalized Conformity Scores for Multi-Output Conformal Regression ICML 2025
Victor Dheur, Matteo Fontana, Yorick Estievenart, Naomi Desobry, Souhaib Ben Taieb
Conformal prediction provides a powerful framework for constructing distribution-free prediction regions with finite-sample coverage guarantees. While extensively studied in univariate settings, its extension to multi-output problems presents additional challenges, including complex output dependencies and high computational costs, and remains relatively underexplored. In this work, we present a unified comparative study of nine conformal methods with different multivariate base models for constructing multivariate prediction regions within the same framework. This study highlights their key properties while also exploring the connections between them. Additionally, we introduce two novel classes of conformity scores for multi-output regression that generalize their univariate counterparts. These scores ensure asymptotic conditional coverage while maintaining exact finite-sample marginal coverage. One class is compatible with any generative model, offering broad applicability, while the other is computationally efficient, leveraging the properties of invertible generative models. Finally, we conduct a comprehensive empirical evaluation across 13 tabular datasets, comparing all the multi-output conformal methods explored in this work. To ensure a fair and consistent comparison, all methods are implemented within a unified code base.
